title: Code review: the decisions still open

steps.intro: Everything you approved is merged except the workspace lock and repo-list work. These three decide how we finish.

steps.headline: Finish this session now and move the remaining work to fresh sessions, or keep going here?
steps.today: This session started on Nov 18. It has survived several computer crashes, and it now remembers its early work only as a summary.
steps.checked: Checked Nov 27: the session restarted from a summary four times; the summary is all that remains of the first week.
steps.problem: A long session loses detail each time it is summarised, so later work leans on a fading memory of what you decided.
steps.proposal: Pick how to carry on. Either way nothing is lost: every leftover item becomes a work card first.

options.label: Wrap up, new sessions
options.summary: I land what is ready, save your deck answers, file one card per leftover item, and give you a one-message starting point for the next session.
pros: Each piece starts with a clean memory and only its own facts.
Smaller sessions are easier for you to follow and check.
cons: You start each new session yourself (one pasted message).

options.label: Keep going here
options.summary: I start the device check next, then the items on the pages after this one.
cons: More detail lost to summaries over time.
One very long thread that is hard to look back through.

steps.path: The workspace lock and repo-list work (youcoded-dev pull request 402)
steps.headline: Merge the self-clearing lock, the single repo list and the test guard now?
steps.today: The work is finished and open for merging. A final independent reviewer swept it for anything a person or a session would notice, and found no blockers.
steps.checked: Checked Nov 27: the final sweep reported SAFE TO MERGE; all tests passed inside the process and memory cage.
steps.problem: Until it merges, a crashed script can still leave a lock that blocks the next session, and the start-up report keeps its own copy of the repo list.
steps.proposal: Yes: I merge once GitHub's checks pass, then clean up. Nobody using the app sees a change. One effect for sessions: a lock left by a crash from before this change still blocks for up to an hour, once. No: it waits.

steps.path: The private release repo: a leftover copy named fix-release-test
steps.headline: Delete the leftover release-repo copy whose fix already reached master another way?
steps.today: A leftover copy and branch hold an earlier version of the release-check fix. The same fix was later merged through a different route.
steps.checked: Checked Nov 27: master no longer reads the deleted games-server workflow, and its release test pins that; the leftover adds nothing master lacks.
steps.problem: Leftover copies make it look as if unfinished release work exists.
steps.proposal: Yes: I delete the copy and its branch, on this computer and on GitHub. No: it stays.

steps.intro: You asked for more explanation on these. Each now says what you would actually notice.

steps.path: Anywhere the app saves a file: settings, themes, chat tags, the project list
steps.headline: Make every save in the app use its one crash-safe saving method?
steps.today: The app has a safe way to save: it writes a complete new copy beside the old one, then swaps them. About 40 places skip it and overwrite the file directly.
steps.checked: From the Nov 18 review, which listed each place; the analytics, theme and fast/effort settings saves were among them.
steps.problem: If the computer crashes or loses power mid-save, the file can be left half-written. The app then reads it as empty and resets that setting to default. Two saves at once can also overwrite each other, losing one change.
steps.proposal: Yes: all 40 use the safe method, and a check refuses new homemade saves. You would notice nothing, except settings no longer resetting after a crash. Lands under your invisible-fix rule, after review. No: fixed only as each one causes trouble.

steps.path: Work cards: the progress notes sessions add
steps.headline: Save card notes to disk at once, but record them on GitHub together when a session pauses?
steps.today: Every card note is recorded on GitHub on its own, the moment it is written. They are almost half of all workspace history entries.
steps.checked: From the Nov 18 review's count (43% of workspace commits); not re-counted since.
steps.problem: Real changes get buried among notes, and sessions trip over each other writing the same file. You worried a crash would lose notes.
steps.proposal: Pick how. Your worry is answered in the first option: nothing waits only in memory.

options.label: Disk now, GitHub later
options.summary: Each note is written to the file at once. They go to GitHub together when the session pauses or ends; any left over after a crash go up at the next session start.
pros: A crash loses no notes: they are already on disk.
About nine in ten fewer history entries.
cons: Notes from a crashed session reach GitHub only when the next session starts on this computer.

options.label: Keep it as today
pros: Every note is on GitHub within seconds.
cons: History stays crowded, and sessions keep colliding on the file.

steps.path: When a settings file is damaged
steps.headline: When a settings file is damaged, should optional things switch off rather than on?
steps.today: When a settings file can't be read, each part of the app picks its own fallback. One known case turned usage reporting back on after you had turned it off; that case is already fixed.
steps.checked: The usage-reporting case was found by the Nov 18 review and fixed in the first hidden-failures batch; no user has reported a damaged file.
steps.problem: Rare: it needs a crash mid-save, a full disk, or a hand edit. Saving safely (above) removes most crashes. But when it happens, a fallback can quietly do the opposite of what you chose.
steps.proposal: Yes: one rule everywhere. A damaged file means optional features and reporting off, lists empty, and the bad copy kept for diagnosis. No: each part keeps its own fallback.

steps.intro: Files on disk, a paired phone, the internet and the marketplace all send the app data it uses as-is.

steps.path: A phone asking the computer to do something
steps.headline: When the computer refuses something a paired phone asked for, should the phone say so?
steps.today: Some phone requests the computer can't accept are dropped without a reply. On the phone the button simply does nothing. Others already show an error; this covers the silent ones.
steps.checked: From the Nov 18 review of the phone link; not re-tested since, so the exact list would be re-checked before any change.
steps.problem: A broken phone action looks like a slow one: you press again, wait, and nobody learns it's a real bug.
steps.proposal: Yes: the phone shows its usual 'that didn't work, try again'. The first release only records refusals, so older phones aren't affected; the next one shows the message. No: keep dropping them.

steps.path: Places in the app that read a file and trust its contents
steps.headline: Add one shared checker for files the app reads, and block new code that skips it?
steps.today: About 320 places read a saved file and use whatever is inside without checking it looks right.
steps.checked: From the Nov 18 review's count of 323; not re-counted since.
steps.problem: A damaged or unexpected file can make a feature misbehave instead of falling back safely, which the damaged-settings question above depends on.
steps.proposal: Yes: one shared checker that falls back safely. New code must use it; the existing places go on a list that can only shrink, fixed in batches. Nobody sees a change. No: a warning only, which tends to get ignored.

steps.page: Rules that a machine could check
steps.intro: Many of my working rules are written down and rely on me remembering them.

steps.headline: Turn written rules into automatic checks, in batches you approve one at a time?
steps.today: Many rules exist only as written instructions, for example: error messages follow the standard, a WHY comment at every edit, and theme files are re-checked when their scripts change.
steps.checked: Examples from the Nov 18 review's root-cause list; the release check that broke on a deleted file was one result.
steps.problem: A written rule gets missed, and nothing notices until something breaks. The release check stopped working this way.
steps.proposal: Yes: I list a batch of rules, what check each becomes, and what would change for you. You approve the batch before I build it. No: rules stay written down.

steps.page: What every session reads at the start
steps.intro: Every session reads about 72 KB of instructions before doing anything. These decide what to trim. Rules you set keep their meaning.

steps.path: The start-up report's three lookup tables (parts of the app, exact files, saved data)
steps.headline: How far should the start-up report's three lookup tables be cut?
steps.today: The report lists every part of the app with its files, about 100 quick-find phrases with their exact file, and every folder the app saves to: 36 KB in every session. Example row: 'the chat transcript / message list → ChatView.tsx'.
steps.checked: Measured Nov 27 from this session's own start-up report: 12.9 KB, 15.3 KB and 7.5 KB. It was 23 KB on Nov 18.
steps.problem: Most sessions use one or two rows, and the tables keep growing: up 13 KB in nine days.
steps.proposal: Pick one. The full tables stay in the map file sessions open when needed.

options.label: One file per row
options.summary: Each row keeps its name and its first file; extra files and notes move to the map.
pros: Saves about 18 KB in every session.
Every row still points straight at the right file.
cons: A session sometimes opens the map for the second file.

options.label: Shorten each row
pros: Keeps more detail in front of each session.
cons: Saves about 10 KB; long rows get cut mid-thought.

options.label: Leave them
cons: Saves nothing, and they keep growing.

steps.path: The how-to sections of the main instructions
steps.headline: Shrink six how-to sections of the main instructions to one pointer line each?
steps.today: Six sections explain how to use tools: question decks, the workbench, screenshots, demo clips, page measuring and model tests. About 3.2 KB in every session. 'New features and UI changes' is not one of the six.
steps.checked: Measured Nov 27 from the main instructions on master.
steps.problem: Most sessions use none of them, but all of them are read every time.
steps.proposal: Pick one. Example pointer: 'Screenshots of named screens: scripts/shoot/README.md.'

options.label: Pointers, keep features
options.summary: The six become one line each. Your approval rules stay in full: the features section, and 'four or more questions go on a deck'.
pros: Every approval rule you set stays word for word.
cons: How-to detail is one step away.

steps.path: The rule against touching your running app
steps.headline: Name both the Windows and Linux places in the rule against touching your running app?
steps.today: The rule forbids touching the app's own files 'under AppData/Roaming/youcoded/' and allows watching it 'with Get-Process or Task Manager'. Both are Windows-only.
steps.checked: Read Nov 27 from the rule on master; the Linux app keeps its files in ~/.config/youcoded/.
steps.problem: You use both Windows and Linux. On Linux a session can't tell which folder the rule protects.
steps.proposal: Yes, exact change: the folder line becomes 'AppData/Roaming/youcoded/ on Windows, ~/.config/youcoded/ on Linux'. The watch line becomes 'Task Manager or Get-Process on Windows; ps or top on Linux'. Nothing else changes. No: leave it.

steps.path: The rule about when to merge
steps.headline: Bring the main instructions' merge rule in line with yours, so the two stop contradicting?
steps.today: Your global rules say: never suggest merging, but ask 'ready to merge?' once you say the work is nearly done. The main instructions say only: merge on explicit instruction, never end a turn suggesting it.
steps.problem: A session following the main instructions never asks 'ready to merge?', even when you've said you're done.
steps.proposal: Yes, new line in the main instructions: 'Merge only on his word. Never suggest it while he iterates; once he says the work is (nearly) done, ask "ready to merge?" (never "ready to push?").' Your global rules stay as they are. No: leave both.

steps.path: The size check on what every session reads
steps.headline: Add a size limit on everything sessions read at the start, so the trimming can't creep back?
steps.today: A check limits the always-read instructions, but it counts only part of them: the main instructions and rules, not the start-up report. It passes while the true total grows.
steps.checked: Measured Nov 27: main instructions 26 KB, your global rules 4 KB, start-up report 42 KB.
steps.problem: Without an honest limit, whatever we trim slowly grows back, as the lookup tables did.
steps.proposal: Pick a limit. A future addition over it would have to trim something else first.

options.label: Limit after the trims
options.summary: Set the limit at the size left after the trims you approve above, plus a small margin.
cons: A big new section would need a trim elsewhere first.

options.label: Limit at today's size
pros: Stops further growth without any trimming.
